opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the hardest problems we have, and it's getting harder as the models get better. Early on you could rely on academic benchmarks: you run MMLU or GSM8K, you see the number go up, and you're reasonably confident you made progress. But those saturate very quickly. Once a model is at 90% plus, the remaining errors are often label noise or ambiguous questions, and you're not learning much anymore.

So during post-training, I think about evaluation in a few layers.

First, you still need fast automatic signals, because you're running a lot of experiments and need to make decisions daily. That means a suite of benchmarks covering reasoning, code, math, multilinguality and so on. But you treat them as a sanity check, a way to catch regressions, rather than the real objective. The danger is overfitting to them, especially when you iterate on data mixtures.

Second, and what really matters for something like a chat model, is human evaluation. You put two models side by side and ask people which response they prefer. That's expensive and slow, and noisy, but it's the closest thing to what users actually experience. The interesting tension is that as models improve, it becomes harder for annotators to judge. If a model writes a complex proof or a long piece of code, an average annotator can't easily tell which is correct. They might prefer the one that looks more confident or is better formatted. So you need expert annotators for some domains, and you have to design the protocol carefully.

Third is using models to evaluate models. Reward models and LLM-as-a-judge are now central. They scale and they're cheap, but they have biases, like preferring longer answers or their own style. So you calibrate them against human judgments and keep checking that the correlation holds as the policy shifts, because the policy will find ways to exploit the judge.

The bigger shift I see is that for the frontier capabilities, reasoning, agents, tool use, you need evaluations where the outcome can be verified. Did the code pass the tests? Did the agent complete the task in the environment? Those are much more robust than asking someone whether they like an answer, and they keep working when the model surpasses the annotator. That's part of why there's so much focus on verifiable tasks and environments now.

Honestly, I'd say evaluation is underrated. People get excited about new training methods, but if you can't measure progress reliably, you're flying blind. A lot of the real research work in post-training is building evals you can trust.

r001.rationale: The response warns that benchmarks can be overfit and should be treated as sanity checks rather than reliable measures of progress.

r002.rationale: It mentions a suite of benchmarks across domains, but does not state that evaluation diversity reduces opportunities for evaluation hacking.

r003.rationale: It says annotators have more difficulty judging stronger models, but does not say that finding prompts that distinguish models becomes harder.

r004.rationale: It describes side-by-side human preference comparisons, but not reusing RLHF annotations to estimate a new model’s win rate against its predecessor.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so evaluation is honestly the hardest part of post-training, and it gets harder as the models get better. When I started working on this, the benchmarks were easy to saturate and you could kind of see the progress. Now, the problem is that the models are better than the benchmarks in a lot of ways, so the signal you get is noisy.

The way I think about it is in layers. First you have the academic benchmarks, things like MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval. They're useful early on to make sure you're not breaking anything, but they saturate quickly and they're often contaminated, so you can't rely on them as your main signal. Second, you have human evaluation, where you take prompts that reflect real usage, you generate answers from your model and from a reference model, and you ask annotators which one is better. That's much closer to what you actually care about, but it's slow, it's expensive, and humans disagree a lot, especially on hard tasks. And third, you have model-as-a-judge, where you use a strong model to compare outputs. That's cheap and fast, but you have to be careful because the judge has biases, it prefers longer answers, it prefers its own style, and you can end up optimizing for the judge rather than for quality.

So in practice we use all three, and the thing we constantly do is check whether they agree. If your reward model or your judge says the new checkpoint is better, but humans don't see it, you have a problem, and usually the problem is that you're reward hacking something.

The other thing I'd say is that as capabilities improve, the bottleneck shifts to the humans. For a lot of tasks, an average annotator can't tell anymore which answer is correct, like in code or math or long reasoning. So you need experts, or you need to design the task so that verification is easier than generation. That's why there's so much interest in verifiable rewards, unit tests for code, checking the final answer in math. Where you can verify, you should, because the signal is clean and it scales. Where you can't, you fall back to preferences, and you accept that it's noisy.

And honestly, one of the most important things is to look at the outputs yourself. Every week, read a few hundred samples. The metrics will tell you something is moving, but they won't tell you why, and it's often by reading the generations that you discover the model has learned some weird shortcut that no benchmark captures.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks saturate and may be contaminated, but does not state that optimizing a model for a benchmark makes its scores less reliable evidence of generalizable capability.

r002.rationale: It discusses several evaluation methods and reading samples, but does not state that diversity in prompts and benchmarks reduces opportunities for evaluation hacking.

r003.rationale: It says models can outgrow benchmarks and that humans may struggle to judge answers, but does not say it becomes harder to find prompts that expose differences between models.

r004.rationale: It describes comparing model answers with a reference in human evaluation, but not reusing RLHF preference annotations to estimate a new model’s win rate against its predecessor.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is that your evaluations have to evolve with the model. Early on, you can measure fairly basic things: does it follow the instruction, is the answer coherent, is it correct? As models improve, those tests saturate. A higher score stops telling you very much about whether you’ve made a better assistant.

So I would look at a combination of things: benchmarks where you can verify the answer, human comparisons on more open-ended tasks, and challenging examples that expose the model’s weaknesses. And you have to be careful about what you’re optimizing. If your evaluator consistently prefers longer answers, you can end up training a model to be more verbose rather than more useful.

The key question is whether the improvement generalizes. Does the model do better on new problems, outside the distribution you used for post-training? That’s much more convincing than improving on the same evaluation you’ve been looking at throughout training.

r001.rationale: The response says that improvement on the same evaluation is less convincing evidence of generalization than improvement on new problems outside the post-training distribution.

r002.rationale: It recommends using varied evaluation methods, but does not state that diversity in prompts and benchmarks reduces evaluation hacking.

r003.rationale: It says basic tests saturate as models improve, but does not clearly say that finding prompts that expose differences between models becomes harder.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss reusing RLHF human preference annotations to estimate a new model’s win rate against its predecessor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is that your evaluation has to evolve with the model. You start with a benchmark, you make progress, and eventually the model saturates it. That doesn’t mean you’ve solved the problem; it means that benchmark is no longer telling you where the model fails.

During post-training, I want a fast feedback loop, but I also want to distinguish improving the score from improving the model. So I would look at several signals: tasks where you can verify the answer, human judgments for more open-ended interactions, and qualitative inspection of failures. If the reward goes up but those independent evaluations don’t improve, that’s something to investigate.

As models become more capable, you need harder tasks and evaluations that reflect how people actually use them. Can the model complete the whole task? Does it recover when something goes wrong? A single aggregate number is useful, but understanding what remains difficult is what tells you what to do next.

r001.rationale: The response says a saturated benchmark no longer reveals where the model fails and distinguishes score gains from model improvement, but it does not state that benchmark optimization makes scores less reliable evidence of generalizable capability.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that using diverse evaluation prompts or benchmarks reduces evaluation hacking.

r003.rationale: It says benchmarks saturate and evaluations should become harder, but does not observe that greater model capability makes it harder to find prompts that distinguish models.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe reusing RLHF human preference annotations to estimate a new model’s win rate against its predecessor.
